title: CCAR-F · Final Review
subtitle: English Q&A · One page · Answers visible · Ordered by review priority

cards.q: Who preserves conversation state between Messages API requests?
cards.a: The application preserves state and resends the messages, tool calls, and tool results needed for coherence; the API keeps no state between requests.

cards.q: How do you preserve exact facts while summarizing a long conversation?
cards.a: Extract and verify exact IDs, amounts, dates, decisions, and customer commitments before summarizing; persist them in a case-facts block outside the summary and inject that block into later requests.

cards.q: How do history, context, structured state, and a summary differ?
cards.a: History is the stored exchange; context is what this request sends to the model; structured state is exact data persisted outside history and reinjected when needed; a summary is compressed history that loses detail.

cards.q: What is the correct mitigation for lost-in-the-middle failures?
cards.a: Put a key-findings summary at the start of the aggregated input and organize detailed results under explicit section headers; metadata alone does not fix the positional effect.

cards.q: What should upstream research agents return when downstream context is limited?
cards.a: Return structured key facts, citations, relevance scores, and source metadata—dates, source locations, and methodological context—instead of verbose content and reasoning; separate content from source URLs, document names, and page numbers so attribution survives the handoff.

cards.q: Which four techniques manage a growing context window?
cards.a: Combine summarization, a structured state object, a sliding window, and selective retention according to what must survive; they are complementary rather than competing techniques.

cards.q: Where should verbose tool results be reduced, and what should remain in context?
cards.a: Trim irrelevant fields in the tool or integration layer before they enter history; then selectively extract-persist-reinject exact facts, summarize decisions and rationale, and remove content that has already served its purpose.

cards.q: Does a sliding window of N turns impose a token or cost limit?
cards.a: No: turns vary in size and early facts fall out of the window, so use a token budget and cut policy together with immediate extraction of durable facts.

cards.q: What are the three legitimate escalation triggers?
cards.a: Escalate for an explicit human request, a policy exception or gap, or inability to make meaningful progress; complexity, frustration, sentiment, and raw self-confidence are not escalation triggers.

cards.q: How should over-escalation and under-escalation be corrected first?
cards.a: Write observable criteria for both escalation and non-escalation, add few-shot examples on both sides of the boundary, and measure precision and recall separately before considering a dedicated classifier.

cards.q: What should the agent do when a lookup returns multiple possible customers?
cards.a: Ask for an additional identifier such as email, tax ID, or order number; never guess by recency or location because selecting the wrong customer can disclose private data.

cards.q: How should exploration findings survive compaction and phase boundaries?
cards.a: Persist exact findings in scratchpads or manifests, inject phase summaries into the next phase's subagents, run directed compaction with preservation instructions, and verify the result item by item before acting.

cards.q: What makes crash recovery safe in a multi-agent pipeline?
cards.a: Persist versioned artifacts and an atomic RunManifest, reconcile task states, artifacts, hashes, and external effects before resuming, treat crashed in_progress work as unfinished, and use idempotency keys or deduplication for side effects.

cards.q: Which three CLAUDE.md levels does the exam test?
cards.a: User level is ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md for personal cross-project preferences; project level is the root or .claude/CLAUDE.md shared through git; directory level is a subdirectory CLAUDE.md loaded while working in that tree.

cards.q: Do CLAUDE.md files override one another?
cards.a: No: applicable files load together and their instructions add up in the session context.

cards.q: Why does a new teammate miss rules stored in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md?
cards.a: That file is personal and outside version control; move shared conventions to the versioned project CLAUDE.md at the repository root or .claude/CLAUDE.md.

cards.q: How do /memory and /context support different diagnoses?
cards.a: Use /memory to locate, open, or create memory files; use /context and its Memory files section to inspect what loaded at session launch.

cards.q: How do you diagnose rules that load only on demand?
cards.a: Reproduce access to a matching file and inspect the terminal's Loaded line or an InstructionsLoaded hook; one launch-time /context call cannot list files that may load later.

cards.q: Does splitting a large CLAUDE.md with @import reduce context by itself?
cards.a: No: @path/to/file modularizes maintenance, but imported content still loads; path-scoped rules are what reduce irrelevant context.

cards.q: How does .claude/rules/ help modularize project guidance?
cards.a: It stores focused, versioned topic files such as testing.md and api-conventions.md instead of one monolithic CLAUDE.md, with optional YAML paths globs for conditional loading.

cards.q: When does a rule with paths enter the context?
cards.a: It loads when Claude works with a matching file through Read, Write, Edit, or a recognized single-file Bash read such as cat or head; loading is not limited to edits.

cards.q: Why use **/*.test.tsx instead of directory CLAUDE.md files for scattered tests?
cards.a: The glob follows the file type across directories, while a directory CLAUDE.md is bound to its own tree; deterministic loading still leaves model adherence probabilistic, so guarantees require code.

lessons.title: Slash Commands, Skills, Permissions, and Plan Mode

cards.q: Where should a team-shared slash command live?
cards.a: Store its Markdown file in the repository's .claude/commands/ directory so git distributes it; ~/.claude/commands/ is for personal shortcuts.

cards.q: How does a skill differ from CLAUDE.md?
cards.a: A skill is an on-demand procedure whose description stays available and whose SKILL.md body loads when used; CLAUDE.md supplies persistent project guidance and is not an occasional workflow.

cards.q: What do context: fork, allowed-tools, and argument-hint do in SKILL.md?
cards.a: context: fork isolates execution in a subagent; on the exam allowed-tools restricts available tools; argument-hint tells the user which parameters to supply.

cards.q: Which skill rules follow the exam guide rather than current product behavior?
cards.a: On the exam, commands and skills are distinct and allowed-tools restricts tools; in the current product they are unified, allowed-tools only pre-approves, and disallowed-tools removes access.

cards.q: How should you personalize a project skill without changing the team's workflow?
cards.a: Create a differently named variant under ~/.claude/skills/; editing or committing personal changes to the project skill would affect everyone.

cards.q: How do you map common needs to the right configuration mechanism?
cards.a: Use project CLAUDE.md for universal standards, a paths rule for file-type conventions, a skill for occasional parameterized workflows, a slash command for a named shared prompt, and a personal command or skill for private shortcuts.

cards.q: When should you use a deny rule versus a PreToolUse hook?
cards.a: Use deny for an unconditional target that matches a tool, command, or path pattern; use PreToolUse when blocking or rewriting depends on conditions such as environment, branch, or amount.

cards.q: How are permission rules evaluated?
cards.a: Evaluation is deny, then ask, then allow, and deny always wins; a personal allow cannot reopen a project deny.

cards.q: What is the settings-file precedence from strongest to weakest?
cards.a: Managed organization policy, command-line arguments, .claude/settings.local.json, project .claude/settings.json, then ~/.claude/settings.json; permission lists combine across files.

cards.q: How do PreToolUse hook decisions and exit codes work?
cards.a: permissionDecision can allow, deny, or ask, updatedInput can rewrite the call, and exit 2 blocks without JSON; exit 1 does not block by default, and a hook allow cannot override a deny or skip an ask.

cards.q: Which hooks fit a formatter and a validator?
cards.a: Run a formatter in PostToolUse after a successful edit; run a blocking validator in PreToolUse before the action executes.

cards.q: When is direct execution preferable to plan mode?
cards.a: Use direct execution for a simple, understood, well-scoped change; per-edit permission prompts already provide supervision and do not turn the task into plan mode.

cards.q: When do plan mode and a multi-phase workflow apply?
cards.a: Use plan mode when design uncertainty requires exploration and approval before edits; use a multi-phase workflow when separate phases produce artifacts and require explicit handoffs and independent human or programmatic gates.

cards.q: What does plan approval authorize, and how is the same plan implemented headlessly?
cards.a: It authorizes implementation, not production or deployment; a later headless run must explicitly resume the session or receive the approved plan artifact and its context, while external release gates remain separate.

cards.q: What is the first fix when an agent confuses two similar tools?
cards.a: Expand and differentiate their descriptions; minimal or overlapping descriptions are the primary cause of unreliable selection, so start there instead of adding routing infrastructure.

cards.q: What belongs in a high-quality tool description?
cards.a: State domain-specific purpose, accepted input formats, example user queries, edge cases, and boundaries that say when to use this tool instead of a similar one.

cards.q: How should severely overlapping tools be redesigned?
cards.a: Rename and specialize them, or split a generic tool into single-purpose tools with clear input and output contracts; names and descriptions both guide selection.

cards.q: What if good tool descriptions still fail around a literal keyword?
cards.a: Inspect the system prompt and rewrite keyword-sensitive routing as intent-based guidance, such as using lookup_order for order-status questions rather than anything containing the word order.

cards.q: Why should each agent receive only role-relevant tools?
cards.a: A smaller scoped tool set reduces semantic overlap, decision complexity, and cross-role misuse; follow least privilege rather than treating any specific tool count as a quota.

cards.q: How do you stop an agent from using a generic tool outside its role?
cards.a: Replace it with a constrained alternative whose handler validates and rejects disallowed targets, such as load_document instead of unrestricted fetch_url; descriptions and schemas alone do not enforce that semantic policy.

cards.q: Can a specialist receive a tool normally associated with another role?
cards.a: Yes, if it is narrowly scoped to a frequent need: give synthesis a limited verify_fact for simple checks while complex investigation still goes through the coordinator to the research agent.

cards.q: How do tool_choice auto, any, and forced selection differ?
cards.a: auto permits text or a tool; any requires some tool while allowing a choice; forced selection requires the named tool, such as extract_metadata.

cards.q: When is tool_choice the right guarantee?
cards.a: Use it when the model must emit a tool_use in this turn; an imperative prompt remains probabilistic, while tool_choice controls the requested emission.

cards.q: Does forced tool selection guarantee successful execution and workflow order?
cards.a: No: tool_choice controls emission, while application code executes the handler and a prerequisite gate validates success and business data before enabling the next step.

cards.q: What is the correct client-tool loop across turns?
cards.a: The model emits tool_use with id, name, and input; the application executes and validates the handler, preserves the assistant block, returns tool_result with the matching tool_use_id, and keeps later steps blocked after failure or invalid output.

lessons.title: Iterative Refinement and Claude Code in CI/CD

cards.q: How do you make an ambiguous transformation converge consistently?
cards.a: Provide 2–3 concrete input/output examples that demonstrate capitalization, null handling, formats, and field names instead of adding more prose.

cards.q: What does test-driven iteration look like?
cards.a: Write tests for expected behavior, edge cases, and performance first; implement, run them, and feed back exact failures with input, expected output, and actual output until the suite passes.

cards.q: When should Claude interview you before coding?
cards.a: Use the interview pattern in an unfamiliar domain so Claude surfaces requirements, constraints, and failure modes you did not know to specify; a longer prompt cannot describe unknown considerations.

cards.q: How should interacting and independent issues be iterated?
cards.a: Put interacting fixes in one detailed message so their shared behavior stays coherent; handle independent fixes sequentially because they do not invalidate one another.

cards.q: Which flag prevents Claude Code from hanging for input in CI?
cards.a: Use -p or --print to process the prompt, write the result to stdout, and exit; shell redirections and timeouts do not provide the same behavior.

cards.q: How do --output-format json and --json-schema work together?
cards.a: The first produces parseable JSON and the second constrains valid structured output; consume the validated structured_output field only after checking that the run succeeded and the field exists with the expected type.

cards.q: What does missing structured_output mean?
cards.a: It means the run did not produce valid structured output, not that there were zero findings; fail the job explicitly instead of substituting an empty findings array.

cards.q: What does dontAsk do in a non-interactive job?
cards.a: It denies calls that would require approval while actions that need no prompt continue; allow rules, allowedTools, and approving hooks can still permit specific calls, so it is not an absolute allowlist.

cards.q: When are bypassPermissions and acceptEdits appropriate?
cards.a: Use bypassPermissions only in an isolated container or VM, with deny rules and denying hooks still effective; use acceptEdits for a code-generation job that may edit in the working directory, not for a read-only reviewer.

cards.q: How do --max-turns and --max-budget-usd contain runaway work?
cards.a: They cap agentic turns and client-estimated spend in -p mode; the budget is not a hard billing cap, and legitimate limit failures call for adjustment or task splitting rather than removing the safeguard.

cards.q: How do --tools, --disallowedTools, and --allowedTools differ?
cards.a: --tools restricts built-ins, --disallowedTools removes built-in or MCP tools, and --allowedTools only pre-approves without restricting availability; removing Edit and Write is insufficient while Bash remains available.

cards.q: What is the shape of a read-only PR-review job?
cards.a: Use -p with dontAsk, --tools Read,Grep,Glob, --disallowedTools mcp__*, turn and budget limits, JSON output and schema, and a prompt that reports rather than fixes findings.

cards.q: How does --bare improve CI reproducibility?
cards.a: It skips automatic discovery of host memory, hooks, skills, plugins, and MCP configuration; supply reviewed context explicitly, for example with --append-system-prompt-file CLAUDE.md, while -p separately controls non-interactive execution.

cards.q: How do Claude Code Action and managed Code Review differ, and how do repeat reviews stay clean?
cards.a: Use the Action with claude_args when you control workflow flags and limits; managed Code Review comments without commits and reads REVIEW.md from the base branch, and every rerun receives prior findings so it reports only new or unresolved issues.

lessons.title: Error Propagation, Human Review, and Provenance

cards.q: What error context should a subagent send to the coordinator?
cards.a: Send structured failure type, attempted query or parameters, partial results, and alternative approaches, with an explicit status such as partial_failure; a vague error string is insufficient for recovery.

cards.q: Which failures should a subagent resolve locally, and what happens next?
cards.a: Handle transient failures locally with backoff or a reformulated query; propagate only unresolved failures with their full context so the coordinator can retry, switch source, re-delegate, or proceed with an annotated gap.

cards.q: How should synthesis handle partial research coverage?
cards.a: Identify well-supported findings and explicitly name areas whose sources failed or remained incomplete; never hide coverage gaps behind fluent prose.

cards.q: Why is high aggregate accuracy insufficient before reducing human review?
cards.a: Aggregate accuracy can hide weak document types and fields; measure performance by document segment and by field before changing the review policy.

cards.q: How does field-level confidence become a calibrated routing signal?
cards.a: Calibrate thresholds on a labeled validation set for each field-by-segment slice; a raw model score is only an input signal, not a probability of correctness.

cards.q: Which conditions independently trigger human review?
cards.a: Low calibrated confidence, an unvalidated segment, ambiguity or contradiction, and high impact are OR conditions: any one is enough, and a high score does not cancel another trigger.

cards.q: When can a field be auto-approved, and what audit still applies?
cards.a: Auto-approve only when no trigger is active and that field-by-segment slice is validated; keep auto-approved fields in a separate stratified random audit sample to measure real errors and support recalibration.

cards.q: How does targeted triage differ from audit sampling?
cards.a: Targeted triage reviews known risks identified by triggers; audit sampling examines auto-approved items to discover missed patterns, so sampling complements rather than replaces triage.

cards.q: How do the extraction reviewer, domain specialist, and authorization owner differ?
cards.a: The extraction reviewer checks the flagged value and necessary excerpt, the domain specialist resolves interpretive ambiguity, and the authorization owner approves high-impact or irreversible action; reviewing data is not authorizing its use.

cards.q: What belongs in a claim-source mapping?
cards.a: Pair each claim with its source URL or document, relevant evidence excerpt, locator where useful, and publication or collection date, and preserve those mappings through synthesis.

cards.q: How should credible sources with conflicting statistics be handled?
cards.a: Preserve both values with their sources and methodological contexts, pass the conflict to the coordinator for reconciliation, and keep the analysis alive rather than choosing, averaging, or discarding evidence.

cards.q: How should dates and certainty appear in the final report?
cards.a: Keep publication_date, using null when unknown, distinguish temporal change from contradiction, separate well-established from contested findings, and render financial data as tables, events as prose, and technical findings as structured lists.

cards.q: Why does hub-and-spoke route subagent communication through the coordinator?
cards.a: Central routing provides observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow; direct subagent-to-subagent channels hide decisions and failures from the coordinator.

cards.q: What are the coordinator's four core responsibilities?
cards.a: Decompose the full query, delegate distinct scopes to the right specialists, aggregate structured results, and dynamically select only the subagents the query requires.

cards.q: All subagents succeeded, but the report covers only one niche. Where is the defect?
cards.a: The coordinator's decomposition was too narrow: the subagents executed their assigned scopes correctly, so fix topic-dimension enumeration and coverage checks in the coordinator.

cards.q: How does an iterative refinement loop close coverage gaps?
cards.a: The coordinator evaluates synthesis for gaps, re-delegates targeted queries with the missing context, reruns synthesis with the new findings, and repeats until coverage is sufficient.

cards.q: What must the coordinator have to spawn subagents on the exam?
cards.a: Its allowedTools must include Task; the current product calls this tool Agent and treats allowedTools as pre-approval, but the exam follows the guide's Task requirement.

cards.q: What does an AgentDefinition configure, and how must it be wired?
cards.a: description guides coordinator selection, prompt defines the specialist's role and output, and tools restricts capabilities; register the definition in the coordinator's agents option because merely declaring it does not make it available.

cards.q: How do you diagnose common subagent-spawning failures?
cards.a: No delegation at all points to missing Task permission; one unavailable agent points to missing wiring; wrong-agent selection points to descriptions; the right agent exceeding its role points to tools and system prompt.

cards.q: What must a self-contained Task prompt include?
cards.a: Include objective, scope and boundaries, complete findings with evidence and source metadata, permitted sources and tools, quality and completion criteria, output schema, and instructions for reporting errors and gaps; subagents inherit neither history nor memory between calls.

cards.q: What must the coordinator verify before accepting a subagent result?
cards.a: Check scope coverage, claim-source attribution, required structure, and declared errors or gaps; fluent prose and a successful tool status do not prove correctness, so re-delegate any explicit gap before aggregation.

cards.q: How do you run independent and dependent subtasks correctly?
cards.a: Emit multiple Task calls in the same coordinator response for independent work; put dependent work in a later turn with all required upstream results explicitly in its prompt.

cards.q: How much autonomy should an open-research subagent receive?
cards.a: Specify objectives, quality criteria, scope, tools, output, and completion contract while leaving search queries and source order adaptable; mandatory procedures still require workflow enforcement and coordinator verification.

cards.q: Which three numbers define the Message Batches API value proposition?
cards.a: It is asynchronous, costs 50% less than synchronous requests, and can take up to 24 hours with no latency SLA.

cards.q: Which workloads belong in batch, and does polling change that decision?
cards.a: Use batch for latency-tolerant, non-blocking work consumed hours later, not real-time replies or merge-blocking checks; polling is normal tracking but neither shortens processing nor creates an SLA.

cards.q: How do you correlate batch requests with out-of-order results?
cards.a: Assign a unique custom_id to each request and match results and failures by the returned custom_id rather than by list position.

cards.q: What is the exam's client-tool limitation for a batch request?
cards.a: A single batch item cannot run the application-driven multi-turn loop of tool_use followed by tool_result; orchestrate that loop outside the item, without generalizing this into a ban on every kind of tool.

cards.q: How often should batches be submitted under a 30-hour delivery SLA?
cards.a: Use submission interval plus 24 hours plus margin within the SLA; the guide's 4-hour interval gives 28 hours total and a 2-hour margin, while 6 hours is the theoretical zero-margin ceiling.

cards.q: How should batch failures and prompt refinement be handled?
cards.a: Fix causes and resubmit only failed custom_id items, and refine prompts on a small synchronous sample before a large run; sample testing improves first-pass success but does not change the 50% discount.

cards.q: Why is an independent review instance stronger than self-review?
cards.a: It receives the diff or code and review criteria without the generator's reasoning history, avoiding the assumptions and self-confirmation bias that extended thinking in the same session cannot remove.

cards.q: How do per-file and cross-file passes address attention dilution?
cards.a: Review each file in a focused pass for local issues, then run a separate integration pass for cross-file contracts and data flow; a larger context window or repeated identical passes does not provide that focus.

cards.q: Why specialize review passes by concern?
cards.a: Security, business logic, and API design examples compete for recall in one prompt, so use independent focused passes with their own few-shot examples and merge their findings.

cards.q: How can confidence route findings after a verification pass?
cards.a: Calibrate confidence thresholds against labeled confirmed and dismissed findings; send low-confidence findings to triage or another pass rather than deleting them, and never treat raw confidence as truth.

lessons.title: Structured Errors, MCP, and Built-In Tools

cards.q: How does an MCP tool communicate failure to the agent?
cards.a: Return a tool result with isError: true and readable error content so the agent can reason about recovery; failure is data, not necessarily a crashed agentic loop.

cards.q: How do transient, validation, business, and permission errors differ?
cards.a: Transient errors warrant backoff or retry; validation requires corrected input; business violations require explanation or escalation without retry; permission failures require credentials, scope, or human intervention.

cards.q: What structured error metadata prevents blind retries?
cards.a: Include errorCategory, isRetryable, and a human-readable description, with a customer-friendly explanation for business violations; Operation failed gives the agent no recovery decision.

cards.q: How does an access failure differ from a valid empty result?
cards.a: A valid empty result is a successful query with no matches; an access failure means the query did not complete and must carry isError plus category and retryability instead of pretending that no data exists.

cards.q: Where are shared and personal MCP servers configured?
cards.a: Use a versioned project-root .mcp.json for servers the whole team needs and ~/.claude.json for personal servers that should not travel through git.

cards.q: How can .mcp.json share configuration without committing secrets?
cards.a: Reference environment variables such as ${GITHUB_TOKEN} instead of hardcoding tokens; the config is shared while each developer supplies the secret locally.

cards.q: What should you check before rewriting an unused MCP tool's description?
cards.a: Run /mcp or claude mcp list to verify connection status, approval, missing environment variables, and exposed tool count; only a connected server with discovered tools can have a selection problem.

cards.q: When should content be exposed as an MCP resource?
cards.a: Expose catalogs such as issue summaries, documentation hierarchies, and database schemas as resources when the agent wastes exploratory calls discovering what exists; tools perform actions while resources provide content visibility.

cards.q: When is a custom MCP server justified?
cards.a: Prefer existing community servers for standard integrations such as GitHub, Jira, Slack, or Postgres; build custom servers for team-specific workflows that existing servers do not cover.

cards.q: How do Grep, Glob, Read, Write, and Edit differ?
cards.a: Grep searches file contents, Glob finds paths by pattern, Read inspects a file or range, Write creates or replaces complete content, and Edit makes a surgical replacement using a unique anchor.

cards.q: What is the reliable fallback when Edit's anchor is not unique?
cards.a: Read the whole file, modify the intended content, and Write it back; do not repeat the same ambiguous Edit or bypass it with sed.

cards.q: How do you explore a large codebase without overstating completeness?
cards.a: Define the question and stopping criterion, narrow candidates with Glob and Grep, read minimal evidence, follow re-exports and local aliases to actual invocations, log file:line evidence and exclusions, and report dynamic or unresolved calls as boundaries rather than absence.

lessons.title: The Agent SDK and the Agentic Loop

cards.q: How do you consume query() and recognize the final Agent SDK result?
cards.a: Iterate query() with async for, handle AssistantMessage blocks while work progresses, and read ResultMessage.subtype for the final outcome; query() is an asynchronous message stream, not one synchronous HTTP response.

cards.q: Who controls the loop in Agent SDK, Messages API, and Claude Code CLI?
cards.a: The Agent SDK manages the loop and built-in tools; a Messages API application executes client tools and returns tool_result itself; Claude Code manages the CLI loop while scripts control flags, context, permissions, and output handling.

cards.q: Which stop_reason values control the basic agentic loop?
cards.a: On tool_use, execute every requested tool, append all matching results to history, and call again; on end_turn, stop and deliver the final response; never infer completion from assistant text.

cards.q: How should other stop_reason values be treated?
cards.a: Treat max_tokens and model_context_window_exceeded as incomplete output, follow the configured rule for stop_sequence, resend the current response to continue after pause_turn, and handle refusal rather than blindly retrying.

cards.q: What is the contract for multiple tool_use blocks in one response?
cards.a: Execute all of them, in parallel when independent, and return every tool_result together in one user message with matching tool_use_id values; failed tools also need results because an unmatched tool_use invalidates the next request.

cards.q: Why can separate user messages for parallel tool results reduce later parallelism?
cards.a: They make the history demonstrate one call per turn; return results together instead, and use disable_parallel_tool_use: true only when serialization is intentional.

cards.q: How do model-driven tool selection and access control coexist?
cards.a: The model chooses which available tool to call and when to stop, while the runtime defines each role's exposed tool perimeter; this differs from a fixed decision tree and does not grant unrestricted access.

cards.q: How do you configure a read-only Agent SDK reviewer?
cards.a: Expose only the required read tools, remove write and shell capabilities with disallowed_tools, and use dontAsk; allowed_tools pre-approves rather than forming a complete allowlist, and the SDK does not load .env automatically.

cards.q: When is a prerequisite gate required instead of stronger prompting?
cards.a: Use a gate whenever identity verification, a value limit, or tool order is mandatory: code blocks downstream execution until the prerequisite is valid, whereas prompt guidance always has a nonzero failure rate.

cards.q: What makes a human handoff actionable without transcript access?
cards.a: Send fixed fields with the verified customer ID, established root cause, amount involved, and recommended action; the human should act without rereading or repeating the diagnosis.

cards.q: How should one message containing several customer concerns be handled?
cards.a: Decompose it into distinct items, investigate them in parallel with the same verified context, and return one unified resolution that closes every item rather than answering only the first.

cards.q: When should a PreToolUse hook intercept a call?
cards.a: Use it before execution to prevent a policy violation and optionally redirect the model with permissionDecision deny and a reason; PostToolUse is too late to undo an action.

cards.q: When is PostToolUse the right normalization mechanism?
cards.a: Use it to transform heterogeneous tool results, such as Unix timestamps and numeric statuses, into canonical values before the model processes them; mechanical normalization belongs in code rather than prompt instructions.

cards.q: When do prompt chaining and dynamic decomposition fit?
cards.a: Use prompt chaining for predictable sequential stages known in advance; use dynamic decomposition for open investigations whose next tasks depend on intermediate discoveries.

cards.q: When should you resume a session versus start fresh?
cards.a: Resume a named session when its context remains valid and identify specific changed files for targeted reanalysis; start fresh with a structured summary when tool results are stale or the codebase changed substantially.

cards.q: When is fork_session the right operation?
cards.a: Use fork_session to explore divergent approaches from one shared analysis baseline; each branch inherits that baseline and then evolves independently.

cards.q: What reduces false positives better than be conservative or high-confidence filtering?
cards.a: Define testable categorical criteria for exactly what to report and what to skip, such as flagging a comment only when its claimed behavior contradicts actual code behavior.

cards.q: What should you do while repairing a review category with many false positives?
cards.a: Temporarily disable that category, rewrite it with explicit criteria and few-shot examples, then re-enable it; noisy categories also erode trust in accurate categories.

cards.q: How do you make severity labels consistent across reviews?
cards.a: Define each severity level with an explicit behavioral criterion and a concrete code example, rather than relying on labels such as major or minor alone.

cards.q: Which project knowledge belongs in persistent review context?
cards.a: Document project conventions, intentionally accepted patterns, and exclusion criteria so every review can distinguish real defects from team decisions and out-of-scope code.

cards.q: Where should persistent and one-off review criteria live?
cards.a: Keep persistent criteria in versioned CLAUDE.md, path-scoped rules, or managed-review REVIEW.md; keep a one-off exception in that run's prompt so it does not affect future reviews.

cards.q: What makes few-shot examples effective?
cards.a: Use 2–4 complete input/output examples targeting ambiguous cases, show why the chosen action beats the plausible alternative, and demonstrate the exact output format rather than adding only obvious examples.

cards.q: How does few-shot reduce hallucination in document extraction?
cards.a: Demonstrate correct extraction across layout and notation variations, including an example that returns null when information is absent instead of inventing a value.

lessons.title: Structured Output, Schemas, and Validation Retry

cards.q: Why is tool use with a JSON schema the exam's most reliable structured-output method?
cards.a: The extraction tool's input_schema makes the model return structured tool input instead of prose, eliminating JSON syntax and formatting failures by construction; strict: true enforces exact schema conformance in the current product.

cards.q: How do prompt formatting, prefill, and tool use differ on the exam?
cards.a: Prompt formatting offers no guarantee, prefill only forces the response to begin inside JSON, and tool use with a strict schema imposes structure; choose according to how much deviation the consumer can tolerate.

cards.q: How should output that grows with input size be prevented from truncating?
cards.a: Split the work into smaller scoped calls with the same schema and merge, deduplicate, and recalculate results in code; raising max_tokens only fits a predictable fixed-size output that barely exceeds a low configured limit.

cards.q: What remains to validate after strict schema validation succeeds?
cards.a: Validate semantics in application code: totals may disagree and values may occupy the wrong fields while remaining schema-valid; schema guarantees shape, not meaning.

cards.q: How should a schema represent missing, ambiguous, or novel source values?
cards.a: Use optional or nullable fields for absent information, unclear for ambiguity, and other plus a detail string for new categories so the schema does not pressure the model to fabricate.

cards.q: Should normalization happen in a hook or in the prompt?
cards.a: Normalize values returned by tools in PostToolUse code; normalize values the model reads from documents with prompt rules and examples alongside the schema, because the error originates in interpretation rather than transport.

cards.q: What makes retry-with-error-feedback effective, and when is it useless?
cards.a: Resend the original document, the failed extraction, and specific validation errors so the model can correct inconsistent fields; if the source lacks the information, supply it or accept null instead of repeatedly pressuring for fabrication.

cards.q: How can a schema support self-correction for inconsistent totals?
cards.a: Extract calculated_total from line items alongside the document's stated_total and set conflict_detected when they disagree, exposing source inconsistency instead of silently choosing one value.

cards.q: Why record detected_pattern on each review finding?
cards.a: Group dismissed findings by the construct that triggered them to identify weak rules and refine the tool from evidence; this records what fired the finding, not how confident the model felt.

cards.q: What are the core numbers and languages of the CCAR-F exam?
cards.a: There are 60 questions in 120 minutes across 4 scenarios drawn from 6, with a passing score of 720 on a 100–1000 scale; the exam is offered in English and Japanese.

cards.q: What should you identify before reading the answer options?
cards.a: Identify the production symptom or the key design requirement, form a root-cause hypothesis, and then find the option that solves that mechanism with the smallest proportional change.

cards.q: How do you choose between a structural mechanism and a prompt refinement?
cards.a: Use code, schemas, hooks, gates, or configuration for deterministic guarantees; use specific descriptions, explicit criteria, and few-shot examples for judgment problems, avoiding both cosmetic patches and over-engineering.

cards.q: How should you handle Select TWO and unanswered questions?
cards.a: Select exactly the requested count and never leave an item blank: wrong guesses carry no additional penalty, so eliminate what you can and choose the most plausible answer.

cards.q: How should you manage the 120-minute clock?
cards.a: Budget about 2 minutes per question; eliminate options, decide, mark uncertainty for review, move on, and return with remaining time rather than sacrificing the pace of later questions.

cards.q: Which identification and technology checks belong before exam day?
cards.a: Bring a valid government-issued photo ID whose name exactly matches the Pearson registration, and run the Pearson VUE tech check on the same machine, network, webcam, microphone, and location.

cards.q: Which exam-day rules protect the session and registration?
cards.a: Keep the desk clear with no notes, second monitor, headphones, or smartwatch; start check-in early, accept the NDA, stay visible without speaking to anyone, and allow 48 hours for cancellation or rescheduling under the current FAQ and policies.
